prompt.context: A Multinational Pharmaceutical and Chemicals manufacturer (German-based) has a 168-person ERP development center. The center was formed 5 years ago by pulling staff from all five corporate divisions. Having completed ERP implementations for more than 50% of its internal business units (5 total, excluding the ERP center itself), the parent company must now decide what to do with this organization going forward.
prompt.question: How would you evaluate the ERP Development Center's situation, and what would you recommend the parent company do with it?

clarifying_info.a: 1995–2003 has been a period of rise and fall with many tribulations for multinationals. Being German-based, the organization is facing a slower economic recovery than the US. Major manufacturing businesses in this space have also seen less turnaround.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors for the ERP development center?
clarifying_info.a: Accenture, SAP, Deloitte, IBM, and a large number of regional and local players. They are all lean, strong, and smart, and are now rebuilding their power by acquiring every client possible. Some are even willing to purchase client relationships.

clarifying_info.q: What does the ERP development center charge?
clarifying_info.a: $100/hour for Technical Analysts and $140/hour for Functional Analysts (rates include T&E).

See the competitor rate datasheet (Exhibit 1) for Developer–SAP, Functional Analyst–SAP, and Technical Analyst–SAP rates across 8 regional companies at Intermediate, Advanced, Manager, and Senior levels.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the customers of the ERP development center?
clarifying_info.a: Five corporate divisions. Three of the five have already had ERP solutions implemented; each implemented division set up its own management and services groups for upgrades, installs, and break-fix work. Significant system changes still require going back to the Development Center. The remaining two divisions will be implemented in the next 12–18 months.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the ERP center relative to the parent?
clarifying_info.a: The ERP center is considered a $30M revenue business within a $5B revenue company (0.6% of parent revenue). It serves only an internal customer base and has no external customer experience.

exhibits.title: Competitor Hourly Rate Datasheet ($/hour)
exhibits.shows: Three rate tables comparing hourly billing rates across 8 competitor companies for three SAP role types (Developer–SAP, Functional Analyst–SAP, Technical Analyst–SAP) at four seniority levels (Intermediate, Advanced, Manager, Senior).

framework: Assess the external market: Who are the competitors, what do they charge, and how does the ERP center compare on price and capability?
Assess internal demand: How much remaining work exists across the 5 divisions, and what happens to demand post-implementation?
Build the revenue model: Headcount × billable rate × utilization = maximum achievable revenue
Build the cost model: Fully-loaded analyst costs + SG&A overhead
Calculate profitability: Compare revenue to costs and stress-test utilization assumptions
Evaluate strategic options: Wind down, restructure for internal needs, expand to external clients, or spin off/sell

questions.prompt: How do the ERP center's rates compare to regional competitors?
questions.guidance: The ERP center charges $100/hr (Technical) and $140/hr (Functional). Regional competitors range broadly. For Functional Analysts most regional players charge $60–$130 Senior; the center's $140 is at or above the high end. For Technical Analysts regional rates are $48–$105; the center's $100 is at the high end. The center is not price-competitive with most regional players for developer/technical roles. A strong answer notes the center also lacks external client experience, compounding the competitive disadvantage.

questions.prompt: Calculate maximum revenue at full utilization (100%) and then at a realistic utilization rate.
questions.guidance: Use headcount, rates, and 1,850 billable hours per year. At 100% utilization: Technical = 34 × $100 × 1,850 = $6,290,000; Functional = 109 × $140 × 1,850 = $28,231,000; Total = $34,521,000. Utilization check: 1,850 / 2,000 = 92.5%. At 80% utilization (more realistic): revenue drops by roughly $6.9M, so ~$27.6M.

math.setup: Billable headcount: 34 Technical Analysts at $100/hr, 109 Functional Analysts at $140/hr. Hours per year = 1,850 (2,000 work hours × 92.5% utilization).
steps: At 80% utilization: $34,521,000 × (80/92.5) ≈ $29,856,000 — a drop of ~$4.7M from stated $30M figure; alternatively stated as ~$7.6M loss vs. break-even
math.answer: Max revenue at 92.5% utilization = ~$34.5M; at 80% utilization = ~$29.9M

questions.prompt: Calculate fully-loaded costs and determine whether the center is profitable.
questions.guidance: Average cost per analyst (143 billable staff) = $220,000 → total analyst cost = $31,460,000. SG&A = $500,000/month × 12 = $6,000,000 (covers the 25 non-billable overhead staff). Total costs = $37,460,000. At 92.5% utilization (revenue $34.5M): loss of ~$2.9M/year. At 80% utilization (revenue ~$26.9M by another calc, per casebook $30M stated − $7.6M loss): loss of ~$7.6M/year. The center is unprofitable at any realistic utilization rate.

math.setup: 143 billable analysts × $220,000 fully-loaded cost + SG&A of $500,000/month × 12 months.
steps: At 80% utilization: loss = approximately −$7.6M per year
math.answer: Operating loss of ~$2.9M/year at 92.5% utilization; ~$7.6M/year at 80% utilization

questions.prompt: What are the strategic options for the ERP Development Center?
questions.guidance: Given that (1) internal demand will fall sharply once the remaining 2 divisions are implemented in 12–18 months, (2) the center is already losing money, and (3) it has no external client experience and is priced at or above market, the viable options are: (a) Wind down — finish implementations and redeploy/rotate staff back into divisions; (b) Restructure as a lean internal IT support function; (c) Attempt external market entry — high risk given price and brand position vs. Accenture/SAP/Deloitte/IBM; (d) Sell or spin off — low likelihood given lack of external track record. The recommended path in the casebook is option (a).

recommendation: Finish the remaining two ERP implementations over the next 12–18 months, then wind down the Development Center in its current form.
Rotate the 168 staff back into the five corporate divisions where their implementation knowledge adds direct value.
Redesign or repurpose any residual corporate IT capability for scaled-down internal needs (upgrades, break-fix) or for potential new activities.
risks: Staff retention may be difficult during a wind-down announcement; key talent could leave before implementations are complete.
The two remaining divisions may face delays if staff morale drops.
If parent company M&A or new system needs arise, losing this capability entirely could be costly to rebuild.
Regional competitors are aggressively acquiring clients; any attempt to pivot to external sales would face steep headwinds.
next_steps: Assess what local/internal customer service needs each division will have post-implementation to size the residual support function.
Evaluate the local market for any niche ERP services the center could offer externally to keep a small team billable.
Consider expanding product/service lines to support the company's own divisions (e.g., analytics, integration) before full closure.
Communicate a clear transition plan to retain key staff through completion of the final two implementations.
